"title": "Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities",

"executive_summary": "This Feature Article reviews the development of bioinspired supramolecular materials that mimic the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies located at bio-interfaces, which are the contact zones between and within cells. The authors argue that a diverse range of cellular activities, including adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation, occur through the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies such as extracellular matrices, phospholipid bilayers, and membrane proteins. Rapid progress in supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology has made it possible to construct and functionalize various bio-interfaces with dynamic natures, and the authors contend that mimicking these dynamic actions can be an effective approach to developing biomaterials applicable to regenerative medicine and drug delivery systems. The article highlights two main material classes: artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming supramolecular materials. The authors introduce recent studies of the development of artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming materials using self-assembling molecules such as fibre-forming amphiphilic peptides, and consider the outlook for the future. The first example concerns stiffness-controlled supramolecular peptide hydrogels as artificial extracellular matrices for enhanced neuronal migration, where A16G and A16G-tagged N-cadherin hydrogels facilitate the migration of neuroblasts into injured neocortex in vivo. The second example concerns peptide fibres capable of efficient incorporation and release of growth factors for neural tissue regeneration, where JigSAP peptides incorporating VEGF promote angiogenesis in a mouse model of ischaemic stroke. The third example concerns redox-responsive supramolecular peptide fibres for kinetics-controlled cargo release, where methionine-containing peptides undergo gel-sol transitions upon oxidation by H2O2. The fourth example concerns highly stable phospholipid membrane nanosheets with self-assembling peptides enabling extended blood circulation, where DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets show prolonged circulation relative to spherical vesicles. The fifth example concerns liposomes undergoing endocytosis-like fission by a membrane-expanding molecular machine for in vivo delivery of viruses, where an amphiphilic molecular machine AzoMEx expands a liposomal membrane to induce outside-in fission and encapsulate M13 phage viruses that retain infectivity after distribution to multiple organs. The authors conclude that these supramolecular approaches to mimicking and controlling bio-interfaces present powerful ways to develop unprecedented regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems, and that the materials science to reconstruct biomimetic interfaces with a dynamic nature is still in its infancy and is expected to make significant progress in the future toward biomedical applications.",

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology); Takahiro Muraoka (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Supramolecular chemistry / biomaterials for regenerative medicine and drug delivery
summary.type_of_paper: Feature Article (review of recent studies with illustrative examples)
summary.executive_summary: This Feature Article reviews the development of bioinspired supramolecular materials that mimic the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies located at bio-interfaces, which are the contact zones between and within cells. The authors argue that a diverse range of cellular activities, including adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation, occur through the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies such as extracellular matrices, phospholipid bilayers, and membrane proteins. Rapid progress in supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology has made it possible to construct and functionalize various bio-interfaces with dynamic natures, and the authors contend that mimicking these dynamic actions can be an effective approach to developing biomaterials applicable to regenerative medicine and drug delivery systems. The article highlights two main material classes: artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming supramolecular materials. The authors introduce recent studies of the development of artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming materials using self-assembling molecules such as fibre-forming amphiphilic peptides, and consider the outlook for the future. The first example concerns stiffness-controlled supramolecular peptide hydrogels as artificial extracellular matrices for enhanced neuronal migration, where A16G and A16G-tagged N-cadherin hydrogels facilitate the migration of neuroblasts into injured neocortex in vivo. The second example concerns peptide fibres capable of efficient incorporation and release of growth factors for neural tissue regeneration, where JigSAP peptides incorporating VEGF promote angiogenesis in a mouse model of ischaemic stroke. The third example concerns redox-responsive supramolecular peptide fibres for kinetics-controlled cargo release, where methionine-containing peptides undergo gel-sol transitions upon oxidation by H2O2. The fourth example concerns highly stable phospholipid membrane nanosheets with self-assembling peptides enabling extended blood circulation, where DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets show prolonged circulation relative to spherical vesicles. The fifth example concerns liposomes undergoing endocytosis-like fission by a membrane-expanding molecular machine for in vivo delivery of viruses, where an amphiphilic molecular machine AzoMEx expands a liposomal membrane to induce outside-in fission and encapsulate M13 phage viruses that retain infectivity after distribution to multiple organs. The authors conclude that these supramolecular approaches to mimicking and controlling bio-interfaces present powerful ways to develop unprecedented regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems, and that the materials science to reconstruct biomimetic interfaces with a dynamic nature is still in its infancy and is expected to make significant progress in the future toward biomedical applications.

The second example concerns peptide fibres capable of efficient incorporation and release of growth factors for neural tissue regeneration, where JigSAP peptides incorporating VEGF promote angiogenesis in a mouse model of ischaemic stroke. The third example concerns redox-responsive supramolecular peptide fibres for kinetics-controlled cargo release, where methionine-containing peptides undergo gel-sol transitions upon oxidation by H2O2. The fourth example concerns highly stable phospholipid membrane nanosheets with self-assembling peptides enabling extended blood circulation, where DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets show prolonged circulation relative to spherical vesicles. The fifth example concerns liposomes undergoing endocytosis-like fission by a membrane-expanding molecular machine for in vivo delivery of viruses, where an amphiphilic molecular machine AzoMEx expands a liposomal membrane to induce outside-in fission and encapsulate M13 phage viruses that retain infectivity after distribution to multiple organs. The authors conclude that these supramolecular approaches to mimicking and controlling bio-interfaces present powerful ways to develop unprecedented regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems, and that the materials science to reconstruct biomimetic interfaces with a dynamic nature is still in its infancy and is expected to make significant progress in the future toward biomedical applications.

Research Context
Bio-interfaces are contact zones where diverse cellular activities occur through dynamic biomacromolecules. Extracellular matrix is a key bio-interface that regulates cellular functions via ligand-receptor interactions. Phospholipid bilayers are essential for substance transportation and signal transduction. Membrane deformation regulates bidirectional substance transportation through exocytosis and endocytosis. Supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology enable construction of dynamic bio-interfaces. Mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces can enable biomaterials for regenerative medicine and drug delivery.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether self-assembling materials can mimic dynamic bio-interfaces for biomedical applications. The hypothesis is that stiffness-controlled peptide hydrogels can enhance neuronal migration after brain injury. The hypothesis is that peptide fibres can incorporate and release growth factors for neural tissue regeneration. The hypothesis is that redox-responsive peptides can control cargo release kinetics. The hypothesis is that stabilized phospholipid nanosheets enable extended blood circulation. The hypothesis is that a membrane-expanding molecular machine enables endocytosis-like fission for virus delivery.

Methodological Details
The article reviews recent studies of bioinspired supramolecular materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces. The review highlights artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming supramolecular materials. Self-assembling peptide fibres are recognized as versatile supramolecular scaffolds of biomaterials. Peptide amphiphiles construct nanofibres by forming cylindrical micelles. Diphenylalanine has been extensively studied as a backbone to afford supramolecular fibres. RADA16 peptides form supramolecular nanofibres through beta-sheet hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interaction. RADA-based peptides can be used as a tag sequence incorporated into proteins of interest with an E. coli expression system. Peptide fibre dynamics can be tuned by amino acid sequences, particularly in the hydrophobic part. Conformational flexibility of peptide fibres can be a critical factor in controlling the stiffness of the hydrogels. Glycine residues generally enhance the conformational flexibility of polypeptide chains. The mammalian brain has a very limited capability of regeneration of lost neurons and regaining function after injury. Promoting the migration of young neurons derived from endogenous neural stem cells is a promising approach.

Procedures And Architectures
A8G is a mutant of RADA16 in which the alanine in the middle of the peptide sequence is replaced with glycine. A16G is a mutant of RADA16 in which the terminal alanine residue is replaced with glycine. Molecular dynamics simulations visualized similar self-assembling morphology of A16G. N-cadherin plays an important role in the migration of neuroblasts along radial glial fibres in the injured neonatal neocortex. Time-lapse imaging of ventricular-subventricular zone neuroblasts was performed on culture dishes coated with A16G or a mixture of A16G and A16G-Ncad hydrogels. Dcx+ is a marker for neuroblasts observed in the hydrogels after injury. JigSAP is a cell-adhesive fibre-forming peptide with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces. JigSAP incorporates JigSAP-tagged vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). AXXXA and GXXXG amino acid sequences are structural motifs found in glycophorin A. These motifs show alpha-helix-to-beta-strand conformational transitions, generating a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface that dimerizes with dovetail packing. JigSAP consists of Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2 sequence and shows one-dimensional self-assembly in aqueous media in silico calculated by MD simulation. When JigSAP (1 wt%) is dispersed in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM), circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopic analysis visualizes a conformational change from helical or coil forms to beta-sheet over 100 hours.

Key Results
A16G forms bundled nanofibres and a more robust hydrogel than RADA16. A16G forms curved fibres seen on transmission electron microscopy. The hydrogel made of A16G showed lower stiffness than that of RADA16. The migration rate of neuroblasts was significantly higher on the hydrogel containing A16G-Ncad than on A16G alone. Dcx+ is abundantly observed in the hydrogel of the mixture of A16G and A16G-Ncad. Neuroblasts are seen sparsely in the hydrogels made of A16G alone and a mixture of A16G and Ncad. JigSAP incorporating JigSAP-tagged vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) shows regenerative therapeutic effects in stroke models without cell transplantation. JigSAP forms nanofibres with an average width of 3.2 nm and length of several micrometres. The JigSAP hydrogel exhibits a remarkably high rigidity of 1.1 x 10^4 Pa. The storage modulus G' and loss modulus G EGFP-JigSAP is incorporated at 93 mol%, whereas non-tagged EGFP is incorporated at only 3 mol%. EGFP-5V is incorporated at 66 mol% and EGFP-RADA16 at 55 mol%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The morphological differences of the fibres could affect the macroscopic properties of the hydrogels. The enhanced mobility with the decreased stiffness and the thixotropic property of A16G hydrogel can be advantageous for injection in biomedical applications. A16G hydrogel containing A16G-Ncad efficiently facilitates the migration of neuroblasts into the injured neocortex in vivo. Fibrous self-assembly of A16G peptide and A16G-Ncad mimics both the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells. The incorporation and releasing property of JigSAP demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release of various full-length growth factors. The JigSAP hydrogel shows more efficient long-term release of the incorporated peptide-tagged proteins than the hydrogels consisting of other self-assembling peptides. The phase transition from gel to sol is useful for drug and cargo release. The self-assembling approach of Chol-MBP is thus advantageous for stabilizing the bicelle morphology to enable prolonged circulation in the blood vessel relative to the spherical vesicles. The membrane-expanding molecular machine AzoMEx functionalizes GUV for endocytosis-like fission, which is useful for encapsulation and delivery of biomacromolecules. These supramolecular approaches to mimicking and controlling bio-interfaces present powerful ways to develop unprecedented regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a Feature Article reviewing recent studies rather than a single experimental study, so specific quantitative results are illustrative rather than from one controlled experiment. The materials science to reconstruct biomimetic interfaces with a dynamic nature is still in its infancy and is expected to make significant progress in the future toward biomedical applications.

Claims
Self-assembling peptide hydrogels can mimic the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells to enhance neuronal migration after brain injury. The migration rate of neuroblasts was significantly higher on the hydrogel containing A16G-Ncad than on A16G alone. Dcx+ is abundantly observed in the hydrogel of the mixture of A16G and A16G-Ncad. A16G hydrogel containing A16G-Ncad efficiently facilitates the migration of neuroblasts into the injured neocortex in vivo. Fibrous self-assembly of A16G peptide and A16G-Ncad mimics both the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells. Neuroblasts are seen sparsely in the hydrogels made of A16G alone and a mixture of A16G and Ncad. This study demonstrates that fibrous self-assembly of A16G peptide and A16G-Ncad mimics both the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells, providing a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy.
Peptide fibres can incorporate and release growth factors for neural tissue regeneration. EGFP-JigSAP is incorporated at 93 mol%, whereas non-tagged EGFP is incorporated at only 3 mol%. The JigSAP hydrogel shows more efficient long-term release of the incorporated peptide-tagged proteins than the hydrogels consisting of other self-assembling peptides. The protein release profile from the gel shows that 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP incorporated into the JigSAP nanofibres is released after 24-hour incubation at 37 degrees C. The percentage of released protein increases to 39 mol% after 168 hours of incubation. The release of EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 stagnates after 48 hours of incubation, and only 5 mol% and 8 mol%, respectively, are released even after 168 hours. The incorporation and releasing property of JigSAP demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release of various full-length growth factors, which should be useful as artificial scaffolds for tissue regeneration.
Redox-responsive supramolecular peptide fibres can control cargo release kinetics. The phase transition from gel to sol is useful for drug and cargo release. Met is a redox-active amino acid that is oxidised by reactive oxygen species such as H2O2, producing methionine sulfoxide (MetO). Upon addition of 30% H2O2 aq. to the top of the hydrogels, the gel-sol transition is induced. JigSAP-IMI-Ox and JigSAP-MII-Ox remain dispersed in solution under a physiological condition, whereas JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII form hydrogels under the same condition. The control of the response rate is an important issue to coincide with the target biological events.
Stabilized phospholipid nanosheets enable extended blood circulation relative to spherical vesicles. Disk-shaped carriers tend to show longer circulation times and stronger adhesion to microvascular networks than spherical carriers. Cu2+-mediated crosslinking of Chol-MBP significantly improves the stability of DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets in the diluted condition. The self-assembling approach of Chol-MBP is thus advantageous for stabilizing the bicelle morphology to enable prolonged circulation in the blood vessel relative to the spherical vesicles. The FL DPPC vesicles were aggregated and clogged, whereas FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in the blood vessels. The self-assembling approach of Chol-MBP is thus advantageous for stabilizing the bicelle morphology to enable prolonged circulation in the blood vessel relative to the spherical vesicles, demonstrating a suitable carrier to the whole body by blood administration.
A membrane-expanding molecular machine enables endocytosis-like fission for in vivo delivery of viruses. The light-triggered mechanical motion of AzoMEx embedded in a 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC)-based giant unilamellar vesicle can expand the liposomal membrane and induce outside-in fission. M13 phages encapsulated into GUVDOPC/AzoMEx were transiently protected from external environments, keeping their infectivity. The membrane-expanding molecular machine AzoMEx functionalizes GUV for endocytosis-like fission, which is useful for encapsulation and delivery of biomacromolecules. A molecular approach that enables endocytosis-like transport where membrane deformation is synchronized with substance transport remains critically unexplored. The AzoMEx-GUV technology to encapsulate M13 phages for protection from immune cells in the blood could be applied to an in vivo phage display method for selection of peptides that bind to ligands in living bodies.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows the typical dynamic functions of the bio-interfaces in cellular activities. Fig. 2a shows the conformational flexibility of peptide fibres can be a critical factor in controlling the stiffness of the hydrogels. Fig. 3a shows the migration rate of neuroblasts was significantly higher on the hydrogel containing A16G-Ncad than on A16G alone. Fig. 4a shows the JigSAP consists of Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2 sequence and shows one-dimensional self-assembly in aqueous media in silico calculated by MD simulation. Fig. 4c shows the JigSAP forms nanofibres with an average width of 3.2 nm and length of several micrometres. Fig. 4e shows the JigSAP hydrogel exhibits a remarkably high rigidity of 1.1 x 10^4 Pa. Fig. 4h shows EGFP-JigSAP is incorporated at 93 mol%, whereas non-tagged EGFP is incorporated at only 3 mol%. Fig. 4k shows the protein release profile from the gel shows that 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP incorporated into the JigSAP nanofibres is released after 24-hour incubation at 37 degrees C. Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of bioinspired supramolecular materials that mimic the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies located at bio-interfaces. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstration that self-assembling peptide hydrogels can enhance neuronal migration after brain injury. 3. The future path is the reconstruction of biomimetic interfaces with a dynamic nature, which is expected to make significant progress in the future toward biomedical applications.
